DOI: [10.7554/eLife.90976.4.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.90976.4.sa1)

In this manuscript, Lee et al. compared encoding of odor identity and value by calcium signaling from neurons in the ventral pallidum (VP) in comparison to D1 and D2 neurons in the olfactory tubercle (OT).

Strengths:

They utilize a strong comparative approach, which allows the comparison of signals in two directly connected regions. First, they demonstrate that both D1 and D2 OT neurons project strongly to the VP, but not the VTA or other examined regions, in contrast to accumbal D1 neurons which project strongly to the VTA as well as the VP. They examine single unit calcium activity in a robust olfactory cue conditioning paradigm that allows them to differentiate encoding of olfactory identity versus value, by incorporating two different sucrose, neutral and air puff cues with different chemical characteristics. They then use multiple analytical approaches to demonstrate strong, low-dimensional encoding of cue value in the VP, and more robust, high-dimensional encoding of odor identity by both D1 and D2 OT neurons, though D1 OT neurons are still somewhat modulated by reward contingency/value. Finally, they utilize a modified conditioning paradigm that dissociates reward probability and lick vigor to demonstrate that VP encoding of cue value is not dependent on encoding of lick vigor during sucrose cues, and that separable populations of VP neuros encode cue value/sucrose probability and lick vigor. Direct comparisons of single unit responses between the two regions now utilize linear mixed effects models with random effects for subject,

Weaknesses:

The manuscript still includes mention of differences in effect size or differing "levels" of significance between VP and OT D1 neurons without reports of a direct comparisons between the two populations. This is somewhat mitigated by the comprehensive statistical reporting in the supplemental information, but interpretation of some of these results is clouded by the inclusion of OT D2 neurons in these analyses, and the limited description or contextualization in the main text.

We appreciate the authors revision of this manuscript and toning down some of the statements regarding "contradictory" results. We still have some concerns about the major claims of this paper which lead us to suggest this paper undergo more revision as follows since, in its present form, we fear this paper is misleading for the field in two areas. here is a brief outline:

(1) Despite acknowledging that the injections only occurred in the anteromedial aspect of the tubercle, the authors still assert broad conclusions regarding where the tubercle projects and what the tubercle does. for instance, even the abstract states "both D1 and D2 neurons of the OT project primarily to the VP and minimally elsewhere" without mention that this is the "anteromedial OT". Every conclusion needs to specify this is stemming from evidence in just the anteromedial tubercle, as the authors do in some parts of the the discussion.

(2) The authors now frame the 2P imaging data that D1 neuron activity reflects "increased contrast of identity or an intermediate and multiplexed encoding of valence and identity". I struggle to understand what the authors are actually concluding here. Later in discussion, the authors state that they saw that OT D1 and D2 neurons "encode odor valence" (line 510). We appreciate the authors note that there is "poor standardization" when it comes to defining valence (line 521). We are ok with the authors speculating and think this revision is more forthcoming regarding the results and better caveats the conclusions. I suggest in abstract the authors adjust line 14/15 to conclude that, "While D1 OT neurons showed larger responses to rewarded odors, in line with prior work, we propose this might be interpreted as identity encoding with enhanced contrast." eliminating "rather than valence encoding" since that is a speculation best reserved for discussion as the authors nicely do.

The above items stated, one issue comes to mind, and that is, why of all reasons would the authors find that the anteromedial aspect of the tubercle is not greatly reflecting valence. the anteromedial aspect of the tubercle, over all other aspects of the tubercle, is thought my many to more greatly partake in valence and other hedonic-driven behaviors given its dense reception of VTA DAergic fibers (as shown by Ikemoto, Kelsch, Zhang, and others). So this finding is paradoxical in contrast to if the authors would had studied the anterolateral tubercle or posterior lateral tubercle which gets less DA input.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.90976.4.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.90976.4.sa3)

Summary:

This manuscript describes a study of the olfactory tubercle in the context of reward representation in the brain. The authors do so by studying the responses of OT neurons to odors with various reward contingencies and compare systematically to the ventral pallidum. Through careful tracing, they present convincing anatomical evidence that the projection from the olfactory tubercle is restricted to the lateral portion of the ventral pallidum.

Using a clever behavioral paradigm, the authors then investigate how D1 receptor- vs. D2 receptor-expressing neurons of the OT respond to odors as mice learn different contingencies. The authors find that, while the D1-expressing OT neurons are modulated marginally more by the rewarded odor than the D2-expressing OT neurons as mice learn the contingencies, this modulation is significantly less than is observed for the ventral pallidum. In addition, neither of the OT neuron classes shows conspicuous amount of modulation by the reward itself. In contrast, the OT neurons contained information that could distinguish odor identities. These observations have led the authors to conclude that the primary feature represented in the OT may not be reward.

Strengths:

The highly localized projection pattern from olfactory tubercle to ventral pallidum is a valuable finding and suggests that studying this connection may give unique insights into the transformation of odor by reward association.

Comparison of olfactory tubervle vs. ventral pallidum is a good strategy to further clarify the olfactory tubercle's position in value representation in the brain.

Weaknesses:

The study comes to a different conclusion about the olfactory tubercle regarding reward representations from several other prior works. Whether this stems from a difference in the experimental configurations such as behavioral paradigms used or indeed points to a conceptually different role for the olfactory tubercle remains to be seen.

claims.claim: Reward related signals are found globally throughout the brain.

claims.claim: OT to VP circuit provides a novel framework in which a high-dimensional encoding of stimulus identity is collapsed onto a low-dimensional encoding of motivational valence.

claims.evidence: Inference based on comparative analysis of OT and VP encoding

results.result: Anatomical tracing reveals that both D1 and D2 neurons of the anteromedial OT project primarily to the lateral VP with minimal projections elsewhere, including VTA. This contrasts with AcbSh projections which target VP, LH, and VTA.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary tracing methods (anterograde AAV and retrograde CTB) consistently demonstrate restricted OT→VP connectivity (C1, C18-C21, C68, C75). The anatomical data are well-controlled with comparison to AcbSh (C73-C74) and include appropriate counterstaining for anatomical boundaries (Figure 1). The findings contradict one prior report but align with another, and the authors provide plausible technical explanations for discrepancies (C108-C109).

results.result: Animals successfully learned odor-sucrose associations and demonstrated flexible reversal learning, with licking accuracy increasing across days and adapting to contingency reversals by day 6.
results.evaluation: Behavioral data clearly demonstrate learning (C22, C24) and reversal (C23) with appropriate statistical analysis (ANOVA with significant effects, C24-C25). The behavioral paradigm successfully decouples identity and valence factors, providing a solid foundation for neural analyses. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=17 animals) and controls for lens placement show no confounding effects (C25).

results.result: VP neurons robustly encode reward contingency in low-dimensional space, with approximately 50% of VP neurons showing valence encoding by day 6. VP neurons respond similarly to odors of the same reward contingency regardless of molecular identity.
results.evaluation: Multiple converging analyses support VP valence encoding: increased responses to sucrose-paired odors (C26-C27, C31), high correlation between responses to different sucrose cues (C34-C35, R²=0.89), predominance of intervalence over intravalence decoding (C39-C40, C42), and categorical classification showing ~48% valence-encoding neurons (C44). The progression across days (C27) and multiple analytical approaches strengthen conclusions. Statistical thresholds are clearly defined (auROC>0.75) and validated against shuffled controls.

results.result: OT neurons primarily encode odor identity rather than reward contingency, with most neurons showing poor single-neuron discriminability and higher correlation for structurally similar odors than for same-valence odors.
results.evaluation: OT encoding contrasts sharply with VP: no increase in dual-S-odor responses across training (C28), preference for single-odor responses (C29), no effect of reward pairing on OTD2 magnitudes (C32), higher correlation for molecular similarity than valence (C36, C38), and majority showing poor discriminability (C46, C89). The comparison between OTD1 and OTD2 is thorough, with OTD2 showing clearest identity encoding. However, the interpretation that OT neurons are "better suited for population code" (C89-C90) requires the dimensionality analysis for full support.

results.result: OTD1 neurons show intermediate encoding properties with some valence modulation but primarily reflect identity encoding with enhanced contrast rather than pure valence encoding.
results.evaluation: OTD1 shows larger responses to rewarded odors (C4, C33) but multiple lines of evidence argue against pure valence encoding: intermediate generalizability between VP and OTD2 (C99), weaker effect sizes than VP (C33), and poor generalization compared to VP (C100). The interpretation as "enhanced contrast" (C107) is reasonable given the data, though somewhat speculative. The distinction from pure valence encoding is well-argued through comparative analysis.

results.result: Longitudinal tracking reveals that sucrose-responsive VP neurons on day 1 become sucrose-cue responsive by day 3, suggesting a Hebbian-like mechanism for reward-cue learning.
results.evaluation: Cell tracking data show ~18-21% of VP neurons responsive to both sucrose (day 1) and sucrose cues (day 3) with same response direction (C47), and 85% of tracked VP neurons show larger responses on day 3 vs day 1 (C48). This is much higher than OT populations. However, the mechanistic interpretation as "Hebbian-like" (C69, C91) is somewhat speculative - the data show correlation but not causation. The tracking methodology appears sound but sample sizes for tracked neurons are not explicitly stated.

results.result: VP encodes information in lower-dimensional space (PR=5.83) compared to OT (PR=9.24-9.61), with VP's first PC sufficient for valence decoding but all 15 PCs required for identity decoding.
results.evaluation: Participation ratio analysis with appropriate subsampling controls (k=15 neurons, C49) shows clear dimensionality differences. PCA-based decoding demonstrates functional consequences: VP's PC1 achieves 85.5% accuracy for valence but requires all PCs for identity (C50-C51), while OT shows opposite pattern (C52). Pairwise distance analyses corroborate these findings (C92-C94). The bootstrapping approach (1000 iterations) provides robust estimates. Statistical comparisons are appropriate.

results.result: VP population decoders generalize well across odor pairs of different reward contingency (95.0±2.0% accuracy), while OTD2 shows negligible generalization and OTD1 shows intermediate generalization (78.5±3.9%).
results.evaluation: Generalization analysis provides strong evidence for abstract valence encoding in VP versus identity encoding in OT. The experimental design (train on one odor pair, test on different pair with same valence relationship) is appropriate for testing generalization (C97-C98). Statistical comparisons show clear differences between regions (C100). This analysis effectively addresses whether populations encode abstract features versus specific stimulus combinations.

results.result: Novel lick-spout retraction paradigm reveals that non-overlapping VP neuron populations encode reward contingency and licking vigor, with both features contributing additively to population-level decoding.
results.evaluation: The lick-spout retraction paradigm successfully decouples reward contingency from motor output (C55). Multiple analyses support segregated encoding: lack of correlation between {Nhi vs NX} and {Lhi vs Nhi} decodability (C56, R²=0.0039, p=0.61), but significant correlation for same-contingency comparisons (C57), and ΔR² regression showing neurons with high valence OR licking values but not both (C58, C105). Linear modeling shows both features contribute (C61, R²=0.23 for combined model vs R²=0.04-0.16 for single features). The use of DeepLabCut for licking detection during spout retraction is methodologically sound.

results.result: Many VP neurons show licking-related activity time-locked to lick-bout onset, with positive correlation between valence and licking decoding ability (R²=0.28, p=2.2×10⁻¹⁰).
results.evaluation: The correlation between valence and licking decoding (C54) is statistically significant and motivated the lick-spout retraction experiment. However, the correlation is moderate (R²=0.28), and the subsequent decoupling experiment (Result 9) demonstrates these are actually separable features encoded by different neurons. This result primarily serves to identify a confound that is then properly addressed experimentally.

results.result: Little evidence for negative valence encoding in VP neurons, with few neurons showing good discrimination of airpuff-cues from control odors (2.3-10.9% with auROC>0.75).
results.evaluation: The lack of negative valence encoding is clearly documented (C43) and acknowledged by authors with plausible explanations: insufficient aversiveness of paradigm (C118) or recording location outside negative-valence VP subregion (C119). Behavioral evidence shows animals perceive the airpuff (C84) but responses are less robust than for sucrose (C83). This is a negative result but important for interpreting the scope of findings. The authors appropriately discuss limitations rather than overclaiming.

results.result: The OT→VP circuit implements a transformation from high-dimensional identity encoding to low-dimensional valence encoding, providing a novel framework for understanding striatopallidal computation.
results.evaluation: This integrative conclusion synthesizes multiple results: anatomical specificity (Result 1), VP valence encoding (Result 3), OT identity encoding (Result 4), and dimensionality differences (Result 7). The framework is well-supported by converging evidence. The information-theoretic interpretation about efficiency vs. robustness tradeoffs (C115-C116) is reasonable. However, the mechanistic proposals about how this transformation occurs (C125-C126) are speculative and not directly tested.

results.result: Discrepancy between single-neuron and population-level decoding: single-neuron intervalence decoding is worse in OT than VP, but population-level intervalence decoding is comparable.
results.evaluation: This observation (C101-C102) is clearly documented and motivates the dimensionality analysis. The discrepancy is real and important for understanding encoding strategies. However, this is primarily a transitional result that leads to the dimensionality analysis (Result 7) rather than a standalone finding. The observation is well-supported by the data presented in Figures 3 and 5.

results.result: The lack of differential OTD1 vs OTD2 projections challenges the direct/indirect pathway dichotomy in ventral basal ganglia.
results.evaluation: This is a logical inference from the anatomical findings (C120-C121) that both OTD1 and OTD2 project primarily to VP with minimal midbrain projections. The conclusion appropriately challenges existing models. However, this is more of a discussion point than a primary experimental result. The authors acknowledge this is speculative and that canonical models may be inadequate (C121).

results.result: Potential explanations for discrepancies with previous studies include regional differences in OT (other parts may have extrapallidal outputs), technical artifacts (viral backflow), or layer-specific differences in recording locations.
results.evaluation: These are speculative explanations (C108-C112) for why results differ from some prior studies, particularly Martiros et al. and Zhang et al. While the speculations are reasonable and the authors appropriately acknowledge limitations, these are not tested hypotheses. The claims are appropriately presented as possibilities rather than conclusions. This represents good scientific practice in discussing discrepancies but doesn't constitute a supported result.

results.result: Proposed mechanistic model: OT provides spatiotemporally precise inhibition to coordinate integration of excitatory inputs onto VP, functioning as a high-dimensional filter rather than driving bulk VP excitation.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic proposal (C122-C126) is speculative and not directly tested. The authors present three possible models and argue for the third based on anatomical considerations (dendritic GABAergic synapses, C124) and the paradox of GABAergic OT neurons and excitatory VP responses. While the reasoning is logical, there are no direct experiments testing synaptic mechanisms, temporal precision, or the proposed filtering function. This is appropriate speculation for the Discussion but not a supported result.

results.result: The authors used anterograde and retrograde tracing to demonstrate that both D1 and D2 neurons of the anteromedial olfactory tubercle (OT) project primarily to the lateral portion of the ventral pallidum (VP) and minimally elsewhere, including the VTA. This contrasts with nucleus accumbens projections which target VP, LH, and VTA.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical concern that the authors make broad conclusions about 'the OT' when their data only covers the anteromedial aspect. The reviewer states 'Despite acknowledging that the injections only occurred in the anteromedial aspect of the tubercle, the authors still assert broad conclusions regarding where the tubercle projects' and requests that 'Every conclusion needs to specify this is stemming from evidence in just the anteromedial tubercle.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges the anatomical findings as 'convincing' and a 'valuable finding,' but the scope limitation issue remains unresolved.

results.result: VP neurons robustly encode reward contingency in low-dimensional space, with responses that increase across training days. VP neurons show high correlation between responses to different sucrose-paired odors (R²=0.89) and preferentially respond to both sucrose odors rather than single odors. By day 6, approximately half of VP neurons were categorized as valence-encoding.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 describes the demonstration of 'strong, low-dimensional encoding of cue value in the VP' as a strength using 'multiple analytical approaches.' Reviewer 3 states 'the dimensionality of neural responses is lower in the VP than in the OT' and that 'VP responses represent values in a more abstract form.' The overall assessment is that 'The results are overall convincing' (Reviewer 3) and the study 'provides insights into how odor information is transformed in the olfactory system.'

results.result: OT neurons (both D1 and D2) primarily encode odor identity in high-dimensional space rather than reward contingency. OTD2 neurons showed no impact of sucrose or airpuff pairing on response magnitudes, while OTD1 showed weaker effects than VP. Most individual OT neurons have little discriminatory information at the single-neuron level but may be better suited for population coding.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 expresses confusion about the interpretation, stating 'I struggle to understand what the authors are actually concluding here' regarding whether OT D1 activity reflects 'increased contrast of identity or an intermediate and multiplexed encoding of valence and identity.' The reviewer notes the authors later state OT D1 and D2 neurons 'encode odor valence' but also acknowledges 'poor standardization' in defining valence. Reviewer 2 finds it 'paradoxical' that the anteromedial OT, which receives dense VTA dopaminergic input, would not greatly reflect valence. The reviewer suggests the abstract should be adjusted to present this as speculation rather than conclusion.

results.result: D1 OT neurons showed larger responses to rewarded odors than other odors, which the authors interpret as identity encoding with enhanced contrast rather than pure valence encoding. The effect size and significance were weaker than observed in VP.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically addresses this interpretation, suggesting the abstract should state 'While D1 OT neurons showed larger responses to rewarded odors, in line with prior work, we propose this might be interpreted as identity encoding with enhanced contrast' and eliminate 'rather than valence encoding' since that is speculation. Reviewer 1 notes 'The manuscript still includes mention of differences in effect size or differing levels of significance between VP and OT D1 neurons without reports of a direct comparisons between the two populations,' indicating some analytical concerns remain.

results.result: Using a novel lick spout retraction paradigm that decouples reward contingency and licking vigor, the authors demonstrate that both features are encoded by largely non-overlapping populations of VP neurons. Reward contingency had a larger and statistically significant correlation with pairwise accuracy than licking vigor.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 describes this as a strength: 'they utilize a modified conditioning paradigm that dissociates reward probability and lick vigor to demonstrate that VP encoding of cue value is not dependent on encoding of lick vigor during sucrose cues, and that separable populations of VP neurons encode cue value/sucrose probability and lick vigor.' No concerns are raised about these specific findings.

results.result: Dimensionality analysis revealed that VP has lower participation ratio (PR=5.83±0.80) than OTD1 (9.24±0.44) or OTD2 (9.61±0.37). The first principal component of VP populations was sufficient for valence decoding but all 15 PCs were required for identity decoding. VP population decoders showed high generalizability across valence comparisons, while OTD2 showed negligible generalizability.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'They show that the dimensionality of neural responses is lower in the VP than in the OT' as a key finding. Reviewer 1 notes the use of 'multiple analytical approaches' as a strength. The dimensionality findings are central to the reviewers' assessment that the study 'provides insights into how odor information is transformed in the olfactory system' (Reviewer 3).

results.result: Animals learned to associate sucrose-paired odors with reward in a flexible manner, showing anticipatory licking behavior that increased in accuracy across days and adapted to contingency reversals by day 6. Learning accuracy was not different across lens-placement groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 describes the behavioral paradigm as 'robust' and notes it 'allows them to differentiate encoding of olfactory identity versus value.' Reviewer 3 calls it a 'clever behavioral paradigm.' No concerns are raised about the behavioral learning data itself.

results.result: Few VP neurons showed strong decoding for airpuff-cues versus control odors (2.3-10.9% with auROC>0.75). Animals showed non-significant trends of behavioral changes to airpuff-cues (less walking, more eye closure) but clear responses to the airpuff US itself.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges these findings about limited negative valence encoding. The authors' own speculation about why this might be (insufficient aversiveness or neurons outside field of view) is not contested by reviewers.

results.result: The authors propose a novel framework for the striatopallidal circuit in which high-dimensional encoding of stimulus identity in OT is collapsed onto low-dimensional encoding of motivational valence in VP. They suggest reward-responsive VP neurons gradually become reward-cue responsive through training.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states this provides 'a novel framework' and that the study 'provides insights into how odor information is transformed in the olfactory system.' Reviewer 1 notes the 'strong comparative approach, which allows the comparison of signals in two directly connected regions' as a strength. The overall framework is accepted, though specific interpretations about OT encoding remain uncertain (see result 3).

results.result: Hierarchical clustering analysis revealed that clusters enriched for VP neurons (clusters I and III) most closely fit the description of valence-encoding neurons, showing similar responses to both sucrose-cues but different responses to sucrose versus puff or control odors.
results.evaluation: This clustering analysis supports the main findings about VP valence encoding and is not specifically challenged by reviewers. It is part of the 'multiple analytical approaches' praised by Reviewer 1.

results.result: The authors propose that the anteromedial OT to VP circuit is an ideal model system for examining transformation of reward cue encoding between connected brain areas. They suggest the lack of OTD1 to midbrain connectivity challenges the dichotomy of direct versus indirect pathways in the ventral basal ganglia.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2's concern about overgeneralizing from anteromedial OT to 'the OT' applies here. The reviewer states this could be 'misleading for the field' and that conclusions should specify they stem from 'evidence in just the anteromedial tubercle.' The theoretical implications about basal ganglia pathways are not directly evaluated by reviewers.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the same anatomical connectivity claims (C1, C18-C21, C68, C73-C79). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED with multiple complementary methods and appropriate controls. Peer review rates it UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 2's concern about overgeneralization from anteromedial OT to 'the OT' broadly, despite Reviewer 3 finding the anatomical findings 'convincing.' The key disagreement is about scope of conclusions rather than data quality.

Both evaluate behavioral learning paradigm (C22-C25, C82). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and adequate sample sizes. Peer reviewers describe the paradigm as 'robust' and 'clever' with no concerns raised about the behavioral data itself. Strong agreement.

Both address VP valence encoding (C2, C26-C27, C31, C34-C35, C37, C39-C40, C42, C44). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with converging analytical evidence. Peer review also finds SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 praising 'strong, low-dimensional encoding' and Reviewer 3 stating 'results are overall convincing.' Strong agreement on VP valence encoding, though peer result also includes cell tracking claims (C47-C48, C91) not in this OpenEval result.

Both evaluate OT identity encoding (C3, C28-C29, C32, C36, C38, C41, C45-C46, C89). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with clear contrast to VP. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 2's confusion about interpretation and concern that conclusions about OT not encoding valence are speculative. Peer reviewer finds it 'paradoxical' given VTA input. Significant disagreement on interpretation confidence.

Both address OTD1 enhanced responses to rewarded odors (C4, C33, C107). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED but notes interpretation as 'enhanced contrast' is somewhat speculative. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 specifically suggesting this should be presented as speculation rather than conclusion in the abstract. Agreement that data exist but interpretation is uncertain.

Both evaluate lick-spout retraction paradigm dissociating valence from motor output (C5, C53-C62, C104-C105). Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval details multiple analytical approaches showing segregated encoding. Peer Reviewer 1 describes this as a strength demonstrating 'separable populations.' Strong agreement on this experimental design and findings.

Both evaluate dimensionality analysis (C49-C52, C92-C94). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate controls and statistical methods. Peer review also finds SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 explicitly stating 'dimensionality of neural responses is lower in the VP than in the OT' as a key finding. Strong agreement. OpenEval R7 also includes generalization analysis (C97-C100) which overlaps with peer R6.

OpenEval R8 focuses on generalization analysis (C97-C100) showing abstract valence encoding in VP versus identity in OT, finding it SUPPORTED. Peer R6 addresses broader dimensionality findings including generalization, also SUPPORTED. Both agree on the strength of these analyses for demonstrating information transformation.

Both address limited negative valence encoding (C43, C83-C84). Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this is a negative result with plausible explanations appropriately discussed. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings. Agreement that the limitation is clearly documented.

Both evaluate the integrative framework about OT-to-VP transformation (C70, C95, C115-C116, C127). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by converging evidence but notes mechanistic proposals are speculative. Peer review also finds SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 calling it 'a novel framework' providing insights into information transformation. Agreement on overall framework value despite some speculative elements.

Both address implications for basal ganglia pathways (C120-C121, C106). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as logical inference but notes it's more discussion than primary result. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 2's concern about overgeneralizing from anteromedial OT. Disagreement stems from scope concerns rather than logic of inference.

OpenEval R6 evaluates cell tracking showing VP neurons responsive to both sucrose and cues (C47-C48, C69, C91), finding SUPPORTED but noting 'Hebbian-like' interpretation is speculative. Peer R2 addresses VP valence encoding broadly and includes these tracking claims (C47-C48, C91) as part of overall SUPPORTED evaluation. Partial overlap with general agreement on data but OpenEval more cautious about mechanistic interpretation.

OpenEval R10 addresses correlation between valence and licking decoding (C53-C54), finding SUPPORTED as motivation for decoupling experiment. Peer R5 focuses on the decoupling experiment itself (C5, C55-C62, C104-C105) which addresses the confound, finding SUPPORTED. These are sequential results where OpenEval R10 identifies the issue that peer R5 (and OpenEval R9) confirm is resolved.

OpenEval R13 addresses the observation that single-neuron and population analyses show different patterns (C101-C102), finding SUPPORTED as transitional result motivating dimensionality analysis. Peer R3 addresses OT identity encoding broadly (C3, C28-C29, C32, C36, C38, C41, C45-C46, C89-C90, C95-C96, C101-C103) with UNCERTAIN rating due to interpretation concerns. Minimal overlap; OpenEval treats this as descriptive observation while peer focuses on interpretation issues.

OpenEval R15 evaluates speculative explanations for discrepancies with prior studies (C108-C112), rating UNCERTAIN as these are untested hypotheses appropriately presented as possibilities. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific methodological speculation claims.

OpenEval R16 evaluates mechanistic proposals about synaptic transformation mechanisms (C122-C126), rating UNCERTAIN as speculative discussion without direct experimental tests. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these mechanistic speculation claims.

Peer R10 addresses clustering analysis (C85-C88) supporting VP valence encoding, finding SUPPORTED as part of 'multiple analytical approaches.' No corresponding OpenEval result specifically evaluates these clustering claims, though they support findings evaluated in OpenEval R3 about VP valence encoding.
